entries.title: Weapons, Oil, AI: Trump Made 1,156 Personal Financial Trades During July
entries.summary: Many of the president’s stock purchases and sales, which span numerous industries, were not disclosed by a federal deadline.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump made 1,156 stock, bond or other financial fund trades in July — a demonstration of his willingness to pursue personal wealth while holding the nation’s highest public office.

Trump disclosed the trades Tuesday in a filing with the Office of Government Ethics. The filing indicates the president, who says financial advisers make trades on his behalf, averaged 77 individual transactions per active trading day. On July 29 alone, Trump made over 300 transactions.

Many of the companies Trump bought or sold stock in are corporate giants that his administration helps regulate or that do business with the federal government.

Trump made trades in companies such as Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta — tech giants that are pursuing artificial intelligence ventures. Trump has been reluctant to heed calls to regulate the industry.

The president also traded shares of major defense contractors, including Palantir, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, GE Aerospace and SpaceX.

Trump also purchased up to $500,000 worth of stock in Axon Enterprise, the manufacturer of Tasers, which has done tens of millions of dollars worth of business with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and U.S. Customs and Border Protection, according to federal records.

Among Trump’s notable stock sales, he dumped a seven-figure amount of Oracle stock over five separate trades. Oracle is a major government contractor, and the company is part of a Trump-brokered deal to place video site TikTok under the control of U.S. corporations.
Oracle.Ellison.Trump (5942x3962, AR: 1.50)The president also traded in a number of oil and gas companies, including ExxonMobil, Chevron and Gulfport. Gas prices have proved to be a headache for Trump as he struggles to bring his nearly seven-month-long war with Iran to a close.

Trump also traded in a number of small municipal bonds, including the Norton County Unified School District 211 in Kansas and the Springtown Independent School District in Texas.

A number of Trump’s trades were disclosed more than 45 days after they were made — in violation of the Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act, which also applies to top officials in the executive branch. It’s not the first time the president has run afoul of the stock trading law.

The dollar values of the trades are disclosed in ranges, not in exact amounts. In July, Trump traded roughly between $70 million and $230 million worth of stock, according to the disclosure.

Trump has long maintained that he is not behind the stock trades made in his name and that financial advisers he’s hired to manage his money have sole discretion over buying and selling stocks and bonds within his portfolio.

“President Trump’s stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement Tuesday to The Washington Sun. “All holdings are maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000,”

“Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold,” Ingle said. “All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers. There are no conflicts of interest.”

But Trump is ostensibly aware of the contents of his portfolio, given that he personally certified his most recent disclosure, which bears his signature.
entries.author: Mark Alfred

entries.title: Vance’s Task Force Strips 750,000 ACA Enrollments Over Accusations of Fraud
entries.summary: Some insurance brokers will also be suspended over accusations that they erroneously enrolled the individuals.
entries.content:
Vice President JD Vance and other Trump administration officials announced Tuesday that the federal government is removing more than 750,000 people from their Affordable Care Act coverage.

The individuals set to be removed from the marketplace were fraudulently enrolled, Vance said. Some insurance brokers will also be suspended over accusations that they erroneously enrolled the individuals.

“We had a system in this country that rewarded brokers that made people rich for enrolling fake people in programs that are meant to ensure that our fellow citizens have health care,” Vance said at a news conference Tuesday. “This was a scandal.”

The Wall Street Journal first reported the enforcement action.

Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz, who runs the agency responsible for enforcing ACA eligibility requirements, announced that there will be a national moratorium on adding any additional brokers to the ACA program for six months.

“We do not feel at all conflicted about that decision because most of the fraud, a disproportionate amount of the fraud, is taking place from these individuals,” Oz said.

The vice president described one instance where the taskforce discovered a ring of 40 broker agents who had allegedly fraudulently funneled 50,000 people into the ACA.

Vance announced the move as part of his anti-fraud task force, which the White House claims has uncovered more than $200 billion in fraud since its inception in March.

The Washington Sun reported last week that the White House’s Fraud Ledger included misleading and unsubstantiated claims, and the government did not provide details about how it calculated the massive clawback of fraudulent funds.

The task force discovered everything from “multinational criminal syndicates” to “small-time hoodlums” involved in this process, Oz said — adding that it's an “open secret” that the fraudsters have been able to use the program “as a piggy bank.”

The Government Accountability Office, an independent agency that conducts research for Congress, found in a July report that CMS needed stronger controls to “protect consumers from unauthorized activity by unscrupulous agents and brokers.”

Rooting out corruption has become an increasingly popular campaign issue ahead of the midterms, as both parties try to cast themselves as being tough on fraud in government programs.

President Donald Trump has targeted the ACA, also known as Obamacare, since his first term — though he has never been able to follow through on his promises to successfully shut down the program. The late Republican Sen. John McCain famously cast the deciding vote against repealing Obamacare when a “skinny repeal of the program” came before Congress in 2017.

In Trump’s second term, the administration has tightened eligibility and enrollment requirements, including additional income verification and tax filing requirements to receive premium subsidies.

ACA enrollment has subsequently fallen sharply and is estimated to continue on a downward trajectory, according to the Kaiser Family Foundation, an organization focused on health policy research and reporting.

entries.title: Trump Appears Surprised to See Kaitlan Collins After White House Ban
entries.summary: “You should not be here,” Trump told the CNN anchor during a trip to the United Nations.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump appeared surprised to see CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins during a trip to the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday following the White House’s decision to expel the network from its credentialed press pool.

“You should not be here covering me,” Trump said after Collins shouted a question at him as he entered the building. “You said you weren't going to cover me. You shouldn't be covering me."

Collins, who has been singled out on multiple occasions by the president in the past, reminded Trump that the U.N. had allowed CNN into the building.

“It's an honor to be here. I'm surprised that CNN is here covering me,” Trump added.

Ultimately, the president turned to Collins, saying: “We're making a lot of progress. Our country is doing really, really well.”

The Trump administration has barred Politico, CNN and MS NOW from White House grounds due to what the president considered unfavorable coverage of the administration and “fake news.”

Over the weekend, the three outlets' credentials were removed, and as a result the five major networks — including CNN, ABC and FOX NEWS — decided to halt White House television pool coverage of the president. The networks collectively maintain the pricey infrastructure needed to broadcast video and audio of the president’s daily activities to countless other news outlets, especially when there is limited space.

On Monday, the fallout from the halt became most apparent. The president, who was scheduled to unveil a newly constructed helipad on the South Lawn, could not be heard as he spoke to officials and construction workers.

The administration’s decision has been challenged in federal court, and the case is expected to have its first hearing on Wednesday. The outlets argue that the president’s ban is unconstitutional under the First Amendment.

entries.title: How a Republican Is Boosting a South Dakota Democrat's Campaign
entries.summary: The Democratic candidate in South Dakota’s secretary of state race received a surprising endorsement from the Republican incumbent.
entries.content:
The South Dakota secretary of state, a Republican, made the surprise decision to cross party lines to endorse a Democrat to succeed her. Now the Democrat is using that to make the case that Republican voters should set aside party affiliations in November.

Terrence Davis, the Democrat running in the solidly red state, told The Washington Sun that he wants to “restore trust” in how election systems work, which he thinks has eroded because of misinformation.

“I believe people want somebody they can trust. They want a government they can trust. That's really what it boils down to,” Davis told The Sun. “My concern is for the voters and the stakeholders here in the state of South Dakota. I trust our system, I trust our elections and I trust our people.”

The sitting secretary of state, Monae Johnson, made the endorsement on Saturday, arguing that voters should make their decision based on policies, not party affiliation.

“I understand that this decision will disappoint some people in my party and anger others. After serving in the Secretary of State’s Office for more than a decade, first as an employee and now as Secretary, I know the difference between campaigning for this office and carrying the responsibility of leading it,” Johnson, who was appointed to her current role by former Gov. Kristi Noem in 2022, said in a statement.

Johnson’s office told The Sun in an email she would “not be providing interviews or additional comment beyond her written statement.”

Davis’ Republican opponent, state Rep. Heather Baxter, was selected for the ballot by delegates rather than through a primary vote. She is campaigning on many of the voting restriction policies that President Donald Trump has pushed for. She wants ballots in South Dakota to be hand counted, a process that could take more time than electronic machines and lead to human errors. Her platform is reflective of one that many Republican candidates for secretary of state are campaigning on this year — election deniers are up for the position in at least three battleground states this year.

South Dakota has passed legislation that reflects Trump’s desire to restrict voting from Washington. The South Dakota SAVE Act, which requires proof of citizenship to vote, was signed into law in March by the governor.

The race is still a long shot for Davis, even with some Republican support, in a state where the Republican Party has maintained a stronghold over statewide office. Johnson’s predecessor, Steve Barnett, won with 65% of the vote in the 2018 midterms.

Davis downplayed the role that party affiliation has to do with the job.

“I used to be a registered Republican,” Davis said. “The secretary of state needs someone that is comfortable talking to everybody at the table, because elections impact Democrats, Republicans and independents, and everybody else in between.”

Baxter argued the opposite in a statement on Monday, reinforcing that party affiliations are important in how people vote.

“A Secretary of State does not write legislation, but does decide whether the office will treat citizenship as an enforceable registration requirement, whether county control will be honored, whether paper and auditability will be treated as essentials or as inconveniences, and whether South Dakota will keep its own election standards or import the national Democratic agenda one administrative decision at a time,” Baxter said after Johnson’s endorsement.

“That is why the letter beside the name matters.”

Davis is a former state trooper and highway patroller. If elected, he would be the first Black person elected to statewide office in the state.

“At this point people are looking for someone they can trust to do the job to the best of their natural ability, protect their constitutional rights, their privacy, and be able to work across party lines,” Davis said.
entries.author: Adora Brown

entries.title: Trump and Xi Meet With the U.S. in an Unfamiliar Position: Weakened
entries.summary: The Iran war and global economic strain have eroded some advantages American officials previously enjoyed in talks between the rivals.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping will meet this week in a show of cordiality between the world’s two most powerful leaders, as they hold their third summit in less than a year. Still, there are serious differences between the Chinese and American positions on issues both sides treat as crucial: China’s trade practices and claims to the self-governing island of Taiwan, U.S. military operations and alliances in East Asia, and competition in their respective development of artificial intelligence.

While U.S. and Chinese officials have endorsed a goal of “constructive strategic stability” — avoiding the mutual damage of outright confrontation — each side is determined to shape future developments on those issues while avoiding big concessions.

Experts say Beijing and Washington appear to have different motivations for their bilateral relationship, with China seeking to be a peer to the U.S., while American policymakers want to retain the global primacy the country has prioritized for decades. Ahead of the summit, global affairs analysts say Trump appears poorly positioned to compete.

The Iran war looms as a shadow over the discussions. Trump’s decision to initiate the offensive and his inability to manage its impact — such as disruptions to the global economy and a spiral of conflict now extending to the other side of the Persian Gulf — have eroded some of the advantages the U.S. has traditionally enjoyed in vying with China, experts argue. Those include a perception of overwhelming military and technological prowess, unique influence over the global economy and a network of strongly committed partners.

“After the Iran war, we see significant gaps in U.S. military power,” Jennifer Kavanagh, an analyst at the Defense Priorities think tank, told reporters in a call last week. “And I don't mean that the U.S. military is weak … but it's fragile. It has limited munitions, has significant gaps in naval and maritime capabilities, and we see that U.S. bases are much more vulnerable than was expected.”

Iran has significantly degraded American military facilities across the Persian Gulf region, and it will take years to rebuild the stockpiles of weapons depleted during the war. The Trump administration has also redirected the sole U.S. aircraft carrier posted in the Pacific Ocean toward the Middle East to replace another carrier that had been under severe strain.

Some observers fear American officials are ignoring those realities and their implications as they approach crucial negotiations with China over pressing matters such as increasing tension with Japan, a U.S. ally.

In policy circles, “There is no sense of needing to acknowledge China’s rise and that we obviously cannot maintain global hegemony given the fact we can’t even control Yemen,” said a congressional staffer in the House of Representatives, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the mood among their colleagues. The staffer was referring to escalating attacks against Saudi Arabia, a key American partner, by the Iran-backed Yemeni militia, the Houthis.

Meanwhile, China remains wary of long-standing American military installations and commitments in the Pacific. To Kavanagh, that leaves the two negotiating in “a very unstable situation,” something she characterized as “the worst of all worlds.”

“You have a situation where the United States has not done enough to show China that it's serious about recognizing Chinese security concerns, but has done enough — or has involuntarily done enough — to freak out allies,” Kavanagh said.

In the immediate term, few expect a flare-up between American and Chinese officials over military deployments or other matters. Trump has unilaterally de-escalated when tensions have risen, such as when China retaliated against the president’s massive tariffs last year by restricting American imports of vital rare earths. And amid the Iran war, Xi is loath to create more instability, while Trump has notably shielded China from the punishment he has promised for Iranian trading partners. A decision on the most contentious issues, like a major U.S. arms sale to Taiwan, could be put off for months.

Melanie Hart, a former State Department official now at the Atlantic Council think tank, predicted the summit will produce modest outcomes: promises of dialogue on AI, lip service that does not end the jockeying over rare earths and another potential truce in the trade war. Hart did note, however, that Xi could be significantly emboldened if Trump further distances himself from the weapons for Taiwan. Another dramatic development isn’t out of the question if, as the New York Times suggested last week, Xi promises to help Trump deepen his relationship with North Korean dictator Kim Jong-Un.

But letting broader American and Chinese disagreements fester could pose a risk, as each side’s relative position in their rivalry continues to shift.

“Some of the defenders of the Trump approach say, ‘Well, he's buying time, he's lowering tensions to buy time.’ But of course the follow-up is: to buy time by doing what, to do what and for what end?” said Julian Gewirtz, a researcher at Columbia University and a White House official in the Biden administration. “Are you buying time so you can launch a war of choice in the Middle East? That is not a good use of buying time and, in fact, is profoundly counterproductive. Or do you buy time to make huge investments in our science and research enterprise and figure out a way to strengthen our alliances?”
entries.author: Akbar Shahid Ahmed

entries.title: Trump Signs Greenland Agreement With Denmark
entries.summary: The president has said the deal would boost U.S. military presence on the island he once hoped to take over entirely.
entries.content:
By Farnoush Amiri and Jamey Keaten

UNITED NATIONS (AP) — President Donald Trump has signed an agreement with Denmark and Greenland aimed at strengthening Arctic and North Atlantic security, easing tensions over his repeated calls for Greenland to become part of the United States.

The signing Tuesday on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York comes days after Trump announced the deal to bolster U.S. military presence on the vast, icy island but keep it under Danish control. The governments provided few details of the agreement before the signing.

For months, Trump has expressed his desire for Greenland to become part of the United States and issued threats to seize the semiautonomous territory from Denmark, a NATO ally.

The US has had a presence in Greenland for many years

Officials from the U.S., Greenland and Denmark negotiated for months behind the scenes, searching for solutions to address some of Trump’s security concerns about the mineral-rich island.

Trump's designs on Greenland strained relations within NATO, with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen warning a U.S. takeover would amount to the end of the Atlantic alliance.

The standoff unsettled many of Greenland's roughly 56,000 people and drove a wedge between the U.S. and Denmark and its European Union partners, who stepped up security exercises on and monetary support for the island.

Trade and hopes for a resource grab have all factored into concerns about Greenland’s future: About two-thirds of its territory sits inside the Arctic Circle, where melting sea ice has opened additional shipping routes

The United States was prominent in Greenland for decades but, since 1945, the U.S. military presence in Greenland has decreased from thousands of soldiers on 17 bases and installations to roughly 200 soldiers on the remote Pituffik Space Base in the northwest. The base supports missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance operations for the U.S. and NATO.

Addressing the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday morning, Trump provided a small window into details of the deal.

"We will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations,” he said, including “building two very major military bases.”

Denmark’s parliament approved a bill last year to allow U.S. military bases on Danish soil, widening a 2023 military agreement made with the Biden administration that gave U.S. troops broad access to air bases in Denmark.

Trump previously insisted the U.S. needed to “take Greenland,” to prevent Russia or China from doing the same. Though Trump said he would rather “ make a deal ” for the territory, he added: “one way or the other, we’re going to have Greenland.”

All parties present the agreement as a positive move

Mikkel Runge Olesen, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute of International Studies, said Greenland and Denmark come away from the deal with the possibility of “ending the crisis without compromising on sovereignty,” while the U.S. gets a “somewhat more favorable” deal than under the existing defense treaty.

But relations overall between the U.S., Denmark and Greenland “are likely to be haunted by this long after Trump leaves office, and the crisis is likely to have significant and lasting negative impact on transatlantic relations more generally,” he said. “The lost trust will take decades to rebuild.”

In a social media post on Saturday, Trump wrote that the emerging agreement “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns.”

In a Danish government statement updated late Monday, Frederiksen said her country was about to “make a great announcement” for Greenland, Denmark and the United States.

She said the deal “recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination.”

Jens-Frederik Nielsen, Greenland’s prime minister, said the deal recognizes Greenland’s interests and will strengthen the security of Greenland, Denmark, the United States “and the Western alliance.”
entries.author: Associated Press

entries.title: Trump Threatens to ‘Annihilate’ Iran at the U.N.
entries.summary: The president delivered an ultimatum to the U.S. adversary that he’s made before, but did it on a much larger stage.
entries.content:
New York — Before the United Nations General Assembly, a stonefaced Iranian representative among them, President Donald Trump had a question about the enemy in the war he had struggled for months to end.

“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before — maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world?” Trump said.”Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”

It was an ultimatum to Iran on the world’s stage: Make a deal or be destroyed.

It wasn’t a new message. Trump delivered a similar one to his audience — and the world — months earlier on Truth Social, writing, “A whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again. I don’t want that to happen, but it probably will.”

It didn’t happen, but the post immediately sparked questions of war crimes and whether the leader of the free world was preparing to commit one. But Tuesday's comments, delivered from a teleprompter, carried new weight.

In a 38-minute address that saw Trump largely stick to the script and avoid weaving off-the-cuff additions, the president’s main target was the same as it has been since the United States initiated a war with Iran in February. Trump defended the actions he’s taken in the Middle East and other aggressive actions taken across the globe. And alongside the blunt words about the world’s leading state sponsor of terror, Trump informed his allies that America had done what they would not. And instead of admonishing those allies for what Trump said was a lack of action, the president instead asked for their help.

“I call on all nations to join us in enforcing the complete economic isolation of Iran until they stop their attacks on commercial shipping, relinquish their nuclear ambitions and cease their support of terror,” Trump said. “If we stand united, we will soon see a world free of the last 51-year menace of Iranian terror.”

His address — and his arrival at the summit — began with domestic issues. Trump’s escalated fight with the press showed up before his remarks, when he told CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins: “You should not be here covering me. You said you weren't going to cover me. You shouldn't be covering me.”

He spoke of low crime rates and the drop in crossings at the southern border, economic investments and tourism, before pivoting to the international problems at hand.  

Even the political fallout from the Iran war, a seemingly intractable issue that’s weighed heavily on Trump’s approval rating, was a brief subject in the president's remarks. Trump predicted Iran would strike a deal after the midterm elections “because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” adding that he doesn’t worry about the war’s impact on the midterms.

“It doesn’t even enter my mind,” Trump said. “The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”

Still, a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Sunday found that 34% of respondents approved of the actions against Iran. Republican support for the war also declined, from 73% in March to 60% in the most recent CNN survey.

Between the new threats to end Iran and criticisms of the UN’s Human Rights Council — “What they do is unbelievable” — Trump returned to another usual target: the U.S.’s own backyard. 

Trump hailed the Venezuelan operation that captured Nicolás Maduro and the subsequent oil deal that concerned Republican lawmakers. He also dedicated a small but significant portion of his remarks to Cuba and affirmed that Secretary of State Marco Rubio was in deep negotiations with the island.

“We’ll not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep, right at our doorstep,” he added.

When Trump mentioned his administration’s efforts to curb Cuban influence, the representatives of Cuba exited the General Assembly Hall. But their disapproval did not stop Trump’s scripted remarks. 

“While others have talked of strength,” Trump said, “I have used it to make America the most powerful in the world.”

But as the address winded down, so did Trump’s dedication to the teleprompter. He debuted his new name for artificial intelligence — “super intelligence” — and wondered whether his influence would be enough to see the change stick. Trump said that all federal documents referencing AI will use the new name.

“We will only encourage super intelligence. We're going to encourage it, not rein it in,” the president said, while acknowledging there will be some Department of Justice oversight of the technology. 

The president delivered his hotly anticipated speech during the morning session of the General Assembly's first official day. Seated in the hall were Rubio, U.N. Ambassador  Mike Waltz, chief of staff Susie Wiles and first lady Melania Trump.

entries.title: Appeals Court Rejects Post-9/11 Restrictions on Capitol Steps Protests
entries.summary: The ruling suggests a rough road ahead for President Donald Trump’s ban on certain media outlets entering the White House grounds.
entries.content:
A policy established in the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks that limited protests on the steps of the U.S. Capitol is unconstitutional, a federal appeals court in Washington ruled Tuesday.

A U.S. Capitol Police rule has for years restricted demonstrations on the building’s East Steps to only allow protests sponsored by a member of Congress. Rev. Patrick Mahoney, a Presbyterian minister in Virginia, challenged the rule in a 2021 lawsuit after being denied access to the area, where he planned to hold a prayer vigil in honor of the 20th anniversary of the terrorist attacks, according to court filings.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit held Tuesday that the Capitol Police Board’s policy infringes on First Amendment free speech protections by offering “preferential treatment” to causes supported by lawmakers. The court concluded that the East Steps of the building are a “nonpublic forum,” meaning the government may pose restrictions, but those limits have to remain “viewpoint neutral” and not let officials exercise discretion over the area’s use.

The current rule “unreasonably allows members of Congress to serve as gatekeepers of speech on the Eastern Steps,” the opinion said. “Because the protection of unpopular speech and advocacy is central to the First Amendment, we cannot leave it to the selective enforcement of members.”

The appellate court partially reversed a D.C. District Court ruling that designated the Eastern Steps as a public forum, a classification that provides the strongest legal protections for protestors by heavily limiting the types of restrictions that can be imposed. The case will go back to D.C. District Court, which is likely to issue a narrow injunction allowing protests to resume.

The ruling reaffirms longstanding First Amendment precedents in D.C. amid a separate battle over access to the White House grounds that is likely to also make it to the appeals court.

President Donald Trump banned Politico, CNN and MS NOW from the White House last week as retribution for publishing what he called “fake news.” Like the East Steps of the Capitol, White House grounds are considered a nonpublic forum where restrictions to access cannot be viewpoint specific.

“Media Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES,” Trump said in a social media post announcing the ban.

The three news organizations filed a lawsuit in D.C. District Court calling the ban a “blatant violation” of “fundamental constitutional principles.”

In a separate social media post following the lawsuit, Trump called media outlets “Third Rate Clowns” with no credibility. He said that his administration anticipates losing in district court and plans to appeal the ruling when it comes.

entries.title: Survival Over Loyalty: Why Republicans Are Breaking With Trump
entries.summary: A string of GOP candidates are publicly disagreeing with the president’s policies or downplaying ties to the president as his approval ratings slide.
entries.content:
A growing number of Republicans are publicly breaking with President Donald Trump, a sign that a party normally in lockstep views him as a liability in the midterms.

In the past week, a Republican congresswoman denounced Trump’s immigration policies, a Republican senator called for a probe into his son’s wedding being funded by a Russian oligarch, and two Republican Senate candidates in battleground states urged him to swiftly end the Iran war.

Staring at the prospect of losing both chambers of Congress, some Trump-backed Republicans are now taking self-preservation measures and backpedaling away from some of the president’s policies that polls have found to be deeply unpopular. Rising fuel and grocery costs are expanding the number of GOP seats in play and prompting more candidates to show some independence.

"President Trump's low approval rates make life tough for Republicans on the ballot,” said Doug Heye, a former communications director for the Republican National Committee. “It's only natural that candidates would seek to create distance from Trump, especially on issues — like the Iran War — that are unpopular. That doesn't guarantee success, and can be a hard needle to thread, but it's the natural play."

Public approval of the Iran war has soured as the seven-month conflict has dragged on. Only 26% of Americans approve of Trump’s handling of the war, according to a CNN poll released Tuesday. Three-quarters of all adults said Trump does not have a clear plan for handling the situation in Iran, and 78% say that he is not doing enough to end the war.

The blowback for Republicans appears particularly acute in Iowa, a red state where farmers are being squeezed by high diesel prices. Three of the state’s four Republican House members called on Trump to wind down the Iran war, including Rep. Ashley Hinson, who’s seeking a seat in the U.S. Senate.

Hinson has repeatedly opposed efforts in Congress to end hostilities with Iran, including last week, but she switched gears this week amid deep voter angst about the economy. In a post on X on Monday, Hinson called on Trump to suspend the gas tax and halt diesel exports, saying that “these actions to lower costs are needed ASAP, and the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end.”

One possible reason for her flip this week is a new poll showing she’s trailing her opponent in the state’s competitive Senate race. Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek led Hinson among registered voters by 50% to 42%, according to an Marist poll released Tuesday. That’s a larger lead than in other surveys, but impressive given that Trump won the state by 13 points in 2024.

Turek called Hinson’s opposition to the war hollow and pointed to her past votes in support of the war.

“When you had the chance to vote to end this war, you chose not to,” he wrote on X. “You voted seven times to continue it, including just last week. It's time to actually end the forever wars and put Iowa and Iowans first.”

In the president’s home state of Florida, Byron Donalds, the Republican candidate for governor, easily fended off primary challenges touting his endorsement from Trump. But this week Donalds, a longtime staunch Trump ally, wiped his campaign website of references to the president’s support.

In Michigan, Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers similarly broke with Trump on Monday by declaring that the war with Iran "needs to end and end quickly.” He appeared in a video recorded at a grocery store and called for more relief for Americans dealing with high costs.

Rogers had previously defended Trump’s Iran war. Abdul El-Sayed, his Democratic opponent, called the former congressman a “liar, coward, [and] fraud.”

Most surveys have shown a close race in Michigan. But a poll released Tuesday by Suffolk University found El-Sayed, a doctor and former public health official, leading Rogers 47% to 40%.

Republican strategists believe every candidate is doing what they must to maximize their chance of winning in November, though that task might be harder for those who have maintained close ties with Trump.

“This is somewhat expected in a tough cycle as campaign teams analyze their place in their race, recognize not a ton can be done to change their fortunes, and throw up a prayer,” said one veteran Republican strategist who requested anonymity to speak freely. “Unless it has been part of your brand for some time, I’m not sure voters will really buy it.”

Michigan Republican strategist Jason Roe said more Republican candidates are likely to distance themselves from Trump in the coming weeks.

“I think it’s a relatively normal thing to happen in any campaign,” he said. “From race to race you are going to see different issues where maybe it’s helpful to separate yourself.”

Still, most elected Republicans continue to stand by Trump, even as their anxiety about the economy and the midterm elections grows. As are most Senate Republican candidates, like Texas attorney general Ken Paxton.

In addition to battleground states like Michigan, Republicans have found themselves facing competitive races in traditionally red states like Kansas, Alaska, Nebraska and Ohio because of growing dissatisfaction over rising costs.

“It's hard out there,” Alaska Sen. Lisa Murkowski said in an interview last week. “I've been talking to a couple of colleagues that come from states where farming is their economy, and farmers are really hurting right now, and they're not particularly pleased with some of what they're seeing with tariffs and the price of diesel, the cost of the Iran [war], and what that means to them.”

The need for Republicans to focus on a new group of contests that weren’t on the radar until recently is making the party increasingly nervous about the president’s impact.

“A year ago, we were talking all happy talk that it was going to be a great year for us,” she added. “I believe that we hold the Senate, but I think it's going to be hard.”

entries.title: Sudanese Leader Denied U.S. Visa Ahead of U.N. General Assembly
entries.summary: Gen. Abdel-Fattah Burhan’s ability to receive the visa reportedly hinges on his approval of a 90-day ceasefire plan negotiated by the U.S.
entries.content:
The Trump administration did not issue an entry visa to Sudan’s de-facto leader ahead of his visit to the United Nations General Assembly this week.

Reversing Gen. Abdel-Fattah Burhan’s visa rejection appears to hinge on his approval of a 90-day ceasefire proposal proposed by Massad Boulos, U.S. senior adviser for Arab and African Affairs, Reuters reported Tuesday morning.

The military commander is still scheduled to speak at the U.N. General Assembly on Thursday, and diplomatic sources in Khartoum told The Sudan Tribune they expect his visa to arrive on Tuesday.

Sudan’s U.N. ambassador, Al-Harith Idriss Al-Harith Mohamed, called for "immediate intervention" in a letter addressed to Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Monday.

“Should this situation persist, it would effectively prevent the Head of State of a Member State of the United Nations from participating in person in the work of the General Assembly,” the letter reads.

In a statement to The Washington Sun, U.N. spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said the secretary-general is “deeply concerned” that Burhan was not issued a visa.

“The full participation of all delegations in the work of the Organization is essential to its proper functioning,” Dujarric wrote. “The Secretariat immediately raised the matter with the United States authorities and continues to engage with them.”

The State Department, the U.N. and Sudan’s U.N. Permanent Mission did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Burhan became Sudan’s de-facto leader after successfully overthrowing President Omar al-Bashir in 2019, and Burhan’s forces conducted a military coup in 2021 that further consolidated his power in the country.

President Donald Trump said in July 2025 that the U.S. would be “facilitating peace” in the country, which has been locked in civil war since April 2023. At the time, Burhan had criticized the proposal, pointing out that other international parties had failed to broker a successful ceasefire, and that the process must not “legitimize” the Rapid Support Forces, the government’s paramilitary group.

The U.S. sanctioned both Burhan and RSF leaders for “destabilizing Sudan” and “undermining the goal of a democratic transition” in January 2025.

The U.S. has denied visas for certain picks for the U.N. delegations in the past due to an individual’s past involvement in security threats and other issues.

President Barack Obama’s administration denied a visa in 2014 for Iran’s pick for U.N. ambassador, Hamid Aboutalebi, citing his alleged involvement in the 1979 U.S. Embassy hostage crisis. The Trump administration also denied visas for Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and other officials this year and in 2025 — though Abbas addressed the assembly via video last year.

entries.title: Trump Says He’s Ordering the Government to Call AI ‘Super Intelligence’
entries.summary: The suggestion came days after industry leaders called for greater government oversight of the emerging technology.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that he has ordered the U.S. government to refer to artificial intelligence in all official documents as “super intelligence.”

“Welcome to the new world of super intelligence — ‘SI’ — let's see if that goes. It sounds much better,” Trump said during his address before the United Nations General Assembly. “The word ‘artificial’ makes intelligence fake. It makes it sound fake, and it is not fake.”

Over the weekend, the president tested different name options through polls on his social media platform Truth Social. Some of the other names included “extreme” intelligence, “supreme” intelligence and “superior” intelligence.

Ultimately, “super” came out on top.

The announcement came days after AI tech leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, called for a slowdown in AI development until proper safety measures could catch up with its rapidly growing capabilities.

The president, for his part, has dismissed the concerns, saying he was the only guardrail artificial intelligence needed.

On Tuesday, he reiterated that message to world leaders instead.

“The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence,” Trump said.

entries.title: Maryland Police Rule the Death of a Man Found Hanging a Suicide
entries.summary: Prince George’s County leaders held an event Monday to offer mental health resources to residents and to quash misinformation about the incident.
entries.content:
Officials with the Prince George’s County Police Department have ruled the death of a Black man found hanging on the side of a road in Upper Marlboro to be a suicide.

In a statement, the department said that detectives who responded to the scene along the 9300 block of D’Arcy Road early Sunday morning immediately opened a death investigation, which included speaking to witnesses and those who knew the man, the statement read.

Based on the preliminary investigation and “learning about his background,” the investigators believe it was a suicide, officials say, with no evidence of foul play found at this time.

The department later noted the trauma the scene may have caused residents.

“We understand this incident is both disturbing and painful to residents who may have driven by the scene or learned about this incident throughout the day,” the statement said.

County leaders held a community event Monday to offer mental health resources and counseling to residents, along with a news conference in which Prince George’s County Executive Aisha Braveboy was joined by other county council members and police officials to quash rumors and misinformation about the incident.

“The community needs and deserves the truth, and we want to provide as much information to the residents as we possibly can,” Braveboy said in the news conference, “respecting the fact that an individual is dead and his family and friends are grieving.”

entries.title: Susan Collins Denies Wrongdoing After Bombshell Report on FBI Corruption Probe
entries.summary: The FBI reportedly investigated ties between Collins’ campaign and a military contractor roughly seven years ago.
entries.content:
Sen. Susan Collins’ office denied any wrongdoing in connection with a bombshell report Tuesday that said the Republican lawmaker had been under scrutiny by the FBI over alleged pay-to-play schemes involving a military contractor.

The investigation, conducted by the nonprofit outlet ProPublica, detailed how Martin Kao, the former chief executive of Navatek, disclosed information to the FBI after his arrest in 2020. He was accused of providing more than $200,000 in illegal campaign contributions to a pro-Collins’ super PAC, which came after Collins helped Navatek secure an $8 million military contract in Maine in 2019.

After Kao volunteered to expose pay-for-play schemes to reduce his prison sentence after pleading guilty, the FBI extensively questioned him about his involvement with Collins, according to the report.

Federal agents had apparently compiled sufficient evidence to open a sweeping investigation into several top lawmakers when President Donald Trump’s overhaul of the Justice Department last year led to the firings of personnel who were working on the case, the report said.

Annie Clark, the deputy chief of staff for Collins, who is currently embroiled in a toss-up race for reelection, wrote on X that the lawmaker’s campaign “was never the target of the FBI investigation.”

Clark also argued that Kao’s track record of fraud and making false submissions makes him untrustworthy. Clark said that Kao “began making outlandish charges” while he awaited sentencing, “deflecting blame from himself and placing it on Senator Collins.”

The FBI did not believe Kao’s statements then and have not contacted Collins’ staff about Kao since 2021, Clark said. The FBI also told ProPublica that federal investigators “found nothing implicating Senator Collins or Senator Collins’ campaign” seven years ago.

“It is important to note that during the Biden Administration the FBI and the Department of Justice thoroughly investigated the Navatek matter,” Clark wrote in the post. ”The Collins campaign cooperated fully with the FBI throughout the investigation, producing all of the documents it requested and serving as fact witnesses in official settings.”

ProPublica reported that Kao met with Scott Reed, the head of Collins’ super PAC, towards the end of 2019 to secure more federal funding in exchange for a donation. Kao reportedly said Navatek would offer a sizable contribution on the condition that Collin knew where the money was coming from and also guarantee the company contracts, to which Reed agreed she would.

Because government contractors cannot make political donations, Kao reportedly used a shell company to send the money, which the FBI noticed and subsequently arrested him for. Kao’s indictment made no reference of wrongdoing on behalf of Collins or her campaign staff.

Reed told ProPublica in an email that he “never had any communications with Senator Collins [or] her staff about Martin Kao and/or Navatek.”

Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee for Maine’s Senate seat, said in a statement the report revealed “corruption of the highest order.” He said Maine needed answers about “every contract and every conversation that Collins and her team facilitated on the backs of taxpayers.”

“The jig is up,” he added.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who is closely affiliated with a super PAC that has donated millions to Collins’ reelection campaign this year, told reporters Tuesday that there has never been any indication that Collins or her campaign were implicated in pay-for-play schemes. He called the report a “political hit job.”

entries.title: Cuba’s Delegation Storms Out of Trump’s U.N. Speech
entries.summary: The delegation’s exit came after Trump’s remarks about the country and its government.
entries.content:
The Cuban delegation abruptly walked out of the United Nations General Assembly during President Donald Trump’s speech Tuesday after he mentioned ongoing negotiations with its government.

“The communist regime is under great pressure, the biggest pressure they've ever been under,” Trump said. “It's an absolutely failed state. It's failing like never before, and it will fall.”

During the speech, Trump outlined the United States’ stance on Cuba, saying its government needed to undertake “fundamental change” and that making those changes remains a top priority of his administration.

But it was not until the president mentioned negotiations between the two countries that the Cuban delegation rushed off the floor.

“[Secretary of State] Marco Rubio is handling a negotiation. He's deep into negotiations with Cuba. Let's see what happens,” Trump said as the delegation walked out.

“We’ll not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep,” the president continued, adding that the State Department had details on the regime’s “ties” to the Communist Party USA and the Democratic Socialists of America.

Under the Trump administration, Cuba has been subjected to increased economic pressure, including tighter sanctions, travel restrictions and measures targeting the island’s access to foreign oil.

The policies have been denounced by leaders across the world, specifically at the U.N.

Just before Trump’s speech, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva took aim at the ongoing crisis Cuba is facing as a result of the draconian economic sanctions.

“In Cuba, the world watches in horror as collective punishment is imposed on 10 million people by an illegal economic and energy embargo,” Lula da Silva said.
entries.author: Raymond Fernández

entries.title: Jurors Are Set to Decide D.C. Council Member Trayon White's Fate
entries.summary: Prosecutors say the video evidence of White exchanging cash is “indisputable,” while the Ward 8 council member’s defense says he didn’t engage in a crime.
entries.content:
Jury deliberations are expected to begin Wednesday in the bribery trial of D.C. Council member Trayon White after both sides delivered their closing arguments Tuesday.

White stands accused of accepting cash bribes from a D.C. government contractor in exchange for agreeing to help him continue to secure lucrative city work.

The Democrat, who represents Ward 8, has maintained his innocence throughout the trial. His defense team does not deny that White accepted the cash, but the jury will soon determine whether the council member agreed to improperly use his position in exchange for money and intended to be influenced by the man who paid him.

Prosecutors argued Tuesday that the case was open and shut.

White “sold his position, his power, his access for his own personal greed,” said Assistant U.S. Attorney Rebecca Ross.

The defense, however, said prosecutors had not done enough to prove that White acted or intended to act corruptly as part of the bribery charge.

“There is no evidence Trayon White has done a corrupt thing, then or ever,” said Gary Kohlman, one of White’s attorneys, in his closing argument.

The outcome of deliberations will indelibly shape White’s future, both personally and politically. If convicted, he faces prison time and would immediately become ineligible for public office in the District. If not convicted, his council colleagues could still vote to expel him if they agree he violated ethics rules.

Pressed on the matter at a news conference Monday, D.C. Council Chairman Phil Mendelson (D) declined to comment on whether he would try to expel White again. After the council last voted to remove him in 2025, White was voted back into office in the special election convened to fill the vacant seat.

***

Much of last week’s testimony focused on a series of videos that show White meeting with an associate named Allieu Kamara during the summer of 2024. Unbeknownst to the council member at the time, Kamara was working with the FBI and allowed authorities to secretly tape their conversations in his car.

Prosecutors used the videos and other evidence to paint White as cash-strapped and corrupt.

“You get to go inside that car and get a front-row seat to the defendant’s crime,” Ross told the jury Tuesday, calling the video evidence “indisputable.”

Prosecutors argue the corrupt relationship between Kamara and White dates to 2019, when Kamara allegedly bribed White in exchange for his help speaking with top city officials about a contract dispute he was having with the D.C. government. Kamara testified that White took the money and agreed to speak with D.C. Mayor Muriel E. Bowser (D) and then-D.C. Attorney General Karl Racine in an effort to prevent the contract termination.

Prosecutors pointed out that in one of his recorded meetings with Kamara, White appeared to reference that situation, telling Kamara that his relationship with Racine was never the same after the pair discussed Kamara’s company, Life Deeds, and that the attorney general had stopped speaking with him.

Five years later, Kamara was arrested on charges of fraud and bribing a different D.C. official, counts to which he later pleaded guilty. He told the FBI about his relationship with White — and prosecutors promised him they would seek a lesser sentence in exchange for his cooperation with an ongoing investigation into White, Kamara and an involved FBI agent testified last week.

In addition to repeatedly pocketing Kamara’s money, White told him he was going to “get to work” and set up meetings with various officials — assuring Kamara he “ain’t going to miss the mark,” Ross said.

And White tried to follow through on those promises, including when the lawmaker met with Office of Neighborhood Safety and Engagement Director Kwelli Sneed, Ross said.

Sneed testified that White had indeed reached out for that meeting, and that it occurred. But she said White only briefly brought up Life Deeds and quickly moved on after Sneed questioned why he was interested in a company that worked outside his ward.

White later told Kamara in a recorded meeting that he could not speak as freely as he wanted to with Sneed because another person was in the room.

Ross argued that this was evidence of White’s intention — and that the council member was guilty of bribery regardless of whether he succeeded in getting Sneed to extend Kamara’s contracts.

The defense argued that White never intended to follow through on what he told Kamara.

Kohlman pointed out instances in which White told Kamara on video that he had met with Racine or D.C. Deputy Mayor for Public Safety and Justice Lindsey Appiah regarding matters related to Kamara’s contracts. Neither official said they could recall such meetings with White during their testimonies. And Sneed testified that White had never actually pressured her to extend contracts for Kamara’s companies, Kolhman said.

White “had no intent other than to look into the status of the contracts,” an action that does not rise to the level of bribery, Kohlman said.

Kohlman also urged jurors to question what Kamara, whom he called a “serial criminal,” said during his testimony. Potentially facing decades in prison, Kamara was “drowning,” and his only choice was to “reach out, grab Mr. White, and drown him instead,” Kohlman said.

While White’s defense attorneys in earlier statements alleged that the government had, through its sting operation with Kamara, possibly induced White to commit a crime he otherwise would not have, they opted against pursuing that argument before the jury on Tuesday. Instead, Kohlman offered a full-throated assertion that there was no crime at all, telling jurors: “There was no offense.”

White opted not to testify, as is his right. But he did speak publicly in a different setting on Tuesday, appearing on Zoom toward the end of the D.C. Council’s breakfast meeting during a break in court proceedings. White was seen on screen from the Wilson Building as he walked around the courthouse and settled for lunch in the cafeteria.

At one point, during a discussion about opioid-related services, White asked the group who currently had a contract with the D.C. government to do that work in Ward 8.

Then — never mind.

“I don’t want to talk about contractors right now,” he said, with a laugh.

Martin Austermuhle contributed to this report.

entries.title: DOJ Charges Utah Postal Worker for Dumping Mail Ballots in Trash During Primary
entries.summary: Seei indicated to authorities that there was no political agenda, and the investigation remains ongoing.
entries.content:
By Mike Catalini

A U.S. Postal Service letter carrier in Utah threw out more than 300 mail ballots that were being sent to voters for the state's June primary, the Justice Department said Tuesday.

Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said during a news conference that 34-year-old Damon Matai Seei was arrested Tuesday and appeared in federal court in Salt Lake City to be arraigned. It wasn’t immediately clear whether Seei had an attorney.

Seei was delivering mail in Eagle Mountain, Utah, when he threw the ballots and other mail into a dumpster in a church parking lot not long after his shift started, McCotter said.

It’s not clear what the motive was, but Melissa Holyoak, the U.S. attorney for Utah, said Seei indicated to authorities that there was no political agenda. The investigation remains ongoing, officials said.

Most voters in Utah cast ballots by mail. Nationwide, nearly a third of voters use mail-in ballots.

Earlier this month, the Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump's attempts to impose new Postal Service rules that would have restricted mail voting for the midterm elections.
entries.author: Associated Press

entries.title: Firm That Handles Trump Social Media Accounts Accuse Co-Founder of Embezzlement
entries.summary: X Strategies, led by Trump adviser Alex Bruesewitz, sued Derek Utley for allegedly siphoning money to fund his gambling addiction.
entries.content:
The political consulting firm that runs President Donald Trump’s social media accounts sued its co-founder in federal court, alleging embezzled and laundered money for his own personal benefit.

The lawsuit, which was filed Friday in Florida, accuses Derek Utley of embezzling at least $5 million from X Strategies, the firm he co-founded with Alex Bruesewitz, a Trump adviser who runs the Trump War Room and Team Trump social media channels.

Utley allegedly used the siphoned money from 2021 to 2026 to gamble at casinos and purchase luxury sports cars, designer clothing, jewelry and first-class travel, according to the lawsuit.

He stepped down from his position at X Strategies in April, according to a court exhibit. Utley is now a partner at advisory firm Tower Strategies, where he leads its communications arm.

The lawsuit, first reported by Politico, seeks to “recover those stolen funds, to hold Utley and his co-conspirators accountable, and to prevent him from causing further harm to X Strategies.”

The lawsuit also named two of Utley’s other businesses: Dicenzo Fitness, which the lawsuit says was used to embezzle money, and Stark Defense Industries, which allegedly holds funds from the consulting firm.

“Utley disguised personal expenditures as business expenses, laundered and gambled stolen funds at casinos (keeping the winnings for himself, if he won, but causing X Strategies to absorb the losses — he lost far more than he won), diverted company funds to personal investments and to Stark Industries and Dicenzo Fitness (entities owned and controlled by Utley), and fabricated financial records to conceal his embezzlement,” the lawsuit reads.

Utley could not be reached for comment. He told Politico that he disputed “these allegations in the complaint and will address them through the legal process. I have no further comment at this time.”

The lawsuit claims that Utley covered up the alleged embezzlement by keeping “incomplete and confusing books” and by fabricating financial records. X Strategies President Michael Seifert initiated an audit after noticing discrepancies with the firm’s finances, the suit says, leading to a confrontation in which Utley initially denied wrongdoing.

He later admitted to Seifert that he “stole millions of dollars from X Strategies,” the suit reads, and “blamed the theft on his low self-esteem, his desire to have more influence and impress others, and his gambling and alcohol addictions.”

entries.title: Trump Backs Ban on Diesel Exports Amid Growing Calls From Republicans
entries.summary: Average diesel prices continue to break records as international conflicts put a strain on the global oil supply.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump backed a ban on U.S. diesel exports Tuesday as pressure from Republicans grows for an embargo on the shipments to curb soaring fuel prices.

The president said he has called for the export prohibition “within my people.”

“I've said let's not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel,” Trump said during a bilateral meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. “That could have a little bit of an effect on regular automobile gasoline, because when you do that, it's a sort of a flow, it's a balance.”

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters the administration is examining “whether it's feasible in terms of the overall refining capacity and whether a full or partial ban would work.”

The average price of diesel continues to break records, clocking in at $6.52 on the AAA fuel prices tracker Tuesday. That’s 70% higher than before the war started Feb. 28.

Some experts argue that a ban could lead to short-term relief while creating long-term issues for the U.S. energy sector by hurting domestic refineries that produce both diesel and gasoline.

“It is always tempting in politics to try a quick fix, especially when you are down and behind in the polls,” former Florida Rep. James Bacchus, an adjunct scholar with the Cato Institute and a professor of global affairs at the University of Central Florida, wrote in a piece published Tuesday. “But this proposed quick fix may not be a fix at all. In some places in the country, it could, despite its intent, lead to even higher prices at the pump.”

Mike Sommers, president and CEO of the American Petroleum Institute, spoke out against the ban in a statement Tuesday, saying it would hurt consumers.

“The answer is more supply and more flexibility — not new restrictions that risk making a difficult situation worse,” Sommers said.

The Heritage Foundation, a conservative public policy research group, is also among the growing number of groups criticizing any possible export ban.

Trump and Zelenskyy spoke about the strain on the fuel source at their meeting during the United Nations General Assembly.

Ukrainian forces have been aggressively striking Russian oil refineries as the 4-year-long war between the countries rages on. Over the weekend, The Financial Times reported that Trump urged Zelenskyy to halt the attacks on the Russian facilities to ease global strain on the price of gas and diesel — a crisis that has been compounded by the Iran war and the conflict over the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump on Tuesday described Ukraine’s attacks on the refineries as a “serious hit” on both Russia and the price of diesel fuel globally, adding that he planned to talk more “about that” with Zelenskyy.

Trump embraced the ban as Republican lawmakers across the country — particularly in the Midwest, where the farming industry plays a major role in the economy — called for the U.S. government to intervene.

Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) joined Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and former Michigan Rep. Mike Rogers’ call for halting U.S. diesel exports.

“American fuel should stay home with Americans,” Sullivan said Tuesday. “The cost of diesel is just too damn high."

Hinson and Rogers, who are running for Senate in their states, have called for the Iran war to end — though Hinson has voted against war powers resolutions that would limit Trump’s ability to take military action without seeking congressional approval, and Rogers has previously made comments supporting the U.S.’s continued efforts in the war.

Sullivan, who’s trying to hold onto his Senate seat, and Grassley have stopped short of calling for the U.S. to bring an end to the war in Iran.

This story has been updated to include statements from the American Petroleum Institute and The Heritage Foundation.

entries.title: The U.S. Will Admit ‘Primarily’ White South Africans as Refugees
entries.summary: The country’s refugee cap will more than double in October for next fiscal year, the State Department informed Congress on Tuesday.
entries.content:
Most of the refugees the United States admits next fiscal year will be white South Africans, the Trump administration informed Congress on Tuesday.

The State Department informed lawmakers that the refugee cap would increase from 7,500 to 17,500 starting in October, according to a notice first reported by CNN. The department will admit “primarily” Afrikaners, people of mostly European descent who President Donald Trump says are being oppressed for being white in what he has called a genocide.

The U.S. has widely denied entry to refugees from the rest of the world since the beginning of Trump's second term. The efforts to prioritize Afrikaners have sparked intense diplomatic friction with the South African government and other international bodies. As of September, all but three of the 12,904 refugees admitted into the U.S. in fiscal year 2026 were from South Africa — a massive increase from the one South African admitted in the fiscal year before Trump took office.

Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio barred South African officials accused of race-based discrimination from entering the United States, claiming they have “not adequately addressed” the administration’s concerns about racially motivated crime against Afrikaners.
